title: pH definition
body: pH = -\log[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.1 EQN: pH = −log[H3O+]

title: pOH definition
body: pOH = -\log[\mathrm{OH^-}]
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.1 EQN: pOH = −log[OH−]

title: Water autoionization constant, Kw
body: K_w = [\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{OH^-}] = 1.0\times10^{-14}\ \text{at } 25^\circ\mathrm{C}
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.2 Water autoionizes with an equilibrium constant Kw

title: pKw, pH and pOH at 25°C
body: pK_w = 14 = \mathrm{pH} + \mathrm{pOH}\ \text{at } 25^\circ\mathrm{C}
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.3 EQN: pKw = 14 = pH + pOH at 25°C

title: Neutral water and temperature
body: A neutral solution has pH = pOH (7.0 only at 25°C), because Kw is temperature dependent, so the pH of pure neutral water deviates from 7.0 at other temperatures.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.3–8.1.A.4 The value of Kw is temperature dependent

title: H+(aq) and H3O+(aq) are interchangeable
body: H3O+(aq) is preferred, but H+(aq) is also accepted on the AP Exam for the aqueous hydrogen ion.
ced_evidence: 8.1.A.1 Hydronium ion and H3O+(aq) are preferred, but H+(aq) is also accepted

title: Strong acids named in the CED
body: Strong acids completely ionize in water, so [H3O+] equals the initial acid concentration.
ced_evidence: 8.2.A.1 (e.g., HCl, HBr, HI, HClO4, H2SO4, and HNO3) will completely ionize

title: Strong base: [OH−] from group I vs group II hydroxides
body: Strong bases (group I and II hydroxides) fully dissociate, so [OH−] equals the initial concentration for a group I hydroxide and double it for a group II hydroxide.
caution: Calculating pOH from [OH−] is not the final step when pH is asked; convert with pH = 14 − pOH (25°C) and report pH.
ced_evidence: 8.2.A.2 double the initial concentration of a group II hydroxide

title: Acid ionization constant, Ka
body: K_a = \dfrac{[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}

title: pKa
body: pK_a = -\log K_a
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.2 EQN: pKa = −log Ka

title: Base ionization constant, Kb
body: K_b = \dfrac{[\mathrm{OH^-}][\mathrm{HB^+}]}{[\mathrm{B}]}

title: pKb
body: pK_b = -\log K_b
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.4 EQN: pKb = −log Kb

title: Conjugate pair: Ka, Kb and Kw
body: K_w = K_a \times K_b \qquad pK_w = pK_a + pK_b
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.6 For any conjugate acid-base pair … Kw = Ka × Kb

title: Weak acid/base: only a small fraction ionizes
body: For a weak acid (base), [H3O+] ([OH−]) is much less than the initial concentration, and most molecules remain un-ionized.
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.1 the vast majority of the acid molecules remain un-ionized

title: Percent ionization
body: The percent of the initial weak acid (or base) that has ionized, calculable from pKa (pKb) and the initial concentration, or from the initial concentration and the equilibrium concentration of any species in the equilibrium expression.
ced_evidence: 8.3.A.5 The percent ionization of a weak acid (or base) can be calculated

title: Strong acid + strong base mixing
body: They react quantitatively, H+(aq) + OH−(aq) → H2O(l), and the pH comes from the concentration of the excess reagent.
ced_evidence: 8.4.A.1 react quantitatively … pH … determined from the concentration of excess reagent

title: Weak acid + strong base: three cases
body: HA(aq) + OH−(aq) → A−(aq) + H2O(l) goes to completion; the pH method depends on which species remains.

items.label: Weak acid in excess
items.meaning: Buffer forms; use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation

items.label: Strong base in excess
items.meaning: pH from moles of excess OH− and total volume

items.label: Equimolar
items.meaning: Slightly basic; pH from A−(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ HA(aq) + OH−(aq)

ced_evidence: 8.4.A.2 If the weak acid is in excess, then a buffer solution is formed

title: Weak base + strong acid: three cases
body: B(aq) + H3O+(aq) → HB+(aq) + H2O(l) goes to completion; the pH method depends on which species remains.

items.label: Weak base in excess
items.meaning: Buffer forms; use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation

items.label: Strong acid in excess
items.meaning: pH from moles of excess H3O+ and total volume

items.label: Equimolar
items.meaning: Slightly acidic; pH from HB+(aq) + H2O(l) ⇌ B(aq) + H3O+(aq)

ced_evidence: 8.4.A.3 If the strong acid is in excess

title: Weak acid + weak base mixing
body: They react to an equilibrium state: HA(aq) + B(aq) ⇌ A−(aq) + HB+(aq).
ced_evidence: 8.4.A.4 react to an equilibrium state

title: Titration curve (pH vs. volume of titrant)
body: A plot of pH against titrant volume used to summarize titration results and locate key points.

items.label: Buffering region
items.meaning: Before equivalence in weak acid/base titrations, where both members of the conjugate pair are present

items.label: Equivalence point
items.meaning: Moles of titrant = moles of analyte originally present

ced_evidence: 8.5.A.1 A titration curve, plotting pH against the volume of titrant added

title: Equivalence point
body: The point in a titration of a monoprotic acid or base where the moles of titrant added equal the moles of analyte originally present, used to obtain the analyte concentration.
caution: Use moles (mol titrant = mol analyte, with the mole ratio) and the equivalence-point volume, not the total volume on the graph.
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.2 the number of moles of titrant added is equal to the number of moles of analyte originally present

title: Half-equivalence point and pKa
body: The point halfway to the equivalence point in a weak acid/base titration, where [HA] = [A−], so pH = pKa and the pKa can be read from the pH there.
caution: Read pKa from the pH at the half-equivalence point, not from the pH at the equivalence point.
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.3 pH = pKa when the conjugate acid and base have equal concentrations

title: pH at the equivalence point by titration type
body: The pH at equivalence is set by the major species in solution.

items.label: Weak acid–strong base
items.meaning: Basic; conjugate base of the weak acid reacts with water

items.label: Weak base–strong acid
items.meaning: Acidic; conjugate acid of the weak base reacts with water

ced_evidence: 8.5.A.4 Strong acid and strong base titrations result in neutral pH at the equivalence point

title: Polyprotic acid titration curves
body: A titration curve of a polyprotic acid shows the number of acidic protons and the pKa for each proton, and the major species at any point can be identified qualitatively.
ced_evidence: 8.5.A.5 titration curves can be used to determine the number of acidic protons

title: Structure and acid/base strength
body: Strong acids have very weak conjugate bases stabilized by electronegativity, inductive effects, resonance, or a combination; strong bases have very weak conjugate acids; electronegative elements stabilize the conjugate base and increase acid strength.
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.1 Electronegative elements tend to stabilize the conjugate base relative to the conjugate acid

title: Common weak acid and weak base classes
body: Classes of weak acids and bases named in the CED.
ced_evidence: 8.6.A.1 Carboxylic acids are one common class of weak acid

title: Predominant form: compare pH to pKa
body: When pH < pKa the acid form (HA) has the higher concentration; when pH > pKa the base form (A−) has the higher concentration.
ced_evidence: 8.7.A.1 When solution pH < acid pKa, the acid form has a higher concentration

title: Acid-base indicator
body: A substance that exhibits different properties, such as color, in its protonated versus deprotonated state, so that property responds to solution pH.
ced_evidence: 8.7.A.2 Acid-base indicators are substances that exhibit different properties

title: Choosing an indicator for a titration
body: Select an indicator whose pKa is close to the pH at the equivalence point.
ced_evidence: 8.7.A.3 indicators should be selected that have a pKa close to the pH at the equivalence point

title: Buffer solution
body: A solution containing a large concentration of both members of a conjugate acid-base pair, in which the conjugate acid reacts with added base and the conjugate base reacts with added acid to stabilize pH.
ced_evidence: 8.8.A.1 A buffer solution contains a large concentration of both members in a conjugate acid-base pair

title: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation
body: \mathrm{pH} = pK_a + \log\dfrac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}
caution: To find the ratio from a given pH, solve [A−]/[HA] = 10^(pH − pKa); do not use ln or e^x, and isolate the ratio.
ced_evidence: 8.9.A.1 EQN: pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA])

title: Why small additions barely change buffer pH
body: Adding small amounts of acid or base does not significantly change the ratio [A−]/[HA], so the buffer pH changes much less than it would without the buffer.
ced_evidence: 8.9.A.1 does not significantly change the ratio of [A−]/[HA]

title: Buffer capacity and component concentrations
body: Raising both buffer component concentrations while keeping their ratio constant keeps pH the same but increases buffer capacity; more conjugate acid gives greater capacity for added base, and more conjugate base gives greater capacity for added acid.
ced_evidence: 8.10.A.1–8.10.A.2 increases the capacity of the buffer to neutralize added acid or base

title: pH-sensitive solubility of salts
body: A salt's solubility is pH sensitive when one of its ions is a weak acid, a weak base, or hydroxide, and the effect is explained qualitatively with Le Châtelier's principle.
ced_evidence: 8.11.A.1 The solubility of a salt is pH sensitive when one of the constituent ions is a weak acid, a weak base, or the hydroxide ion
